paragraphs.text: Commentary § 4.33:1 Rule 4.33 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 4.33. 1. A Brief Overview In Abou Shaaban v. Baljak, 2024 ABKB 28, additional reasons 2024 ABKB 125, Justice Marion provided this useful summary of the law: [60] The relevant period of delay must be determined by starting with the last uncontroversial significant advance up to the date the dismissal application was filed (not the date it was heard): Rahmani v 959630 Alberta Ltd, 2021 ABCA 110 at paras 16-17; Vanmaele Estate (Re), 2023 ABKB 456 at para 21; Taschuk v Taschuk, 2022 ABKB 786 at para 13; Babiuk v Heap, 2023 ABKB 410 at para 48. A question to be asked is: “was there a three year period between these dates without any significant advance in the action?”: Rahmani at para 17. If the relevant period of delay includes March 17, 2020 to June 1, 2020, then Ministerial Order 27/2020 must be considered, as it suspended the operation of time limits under the Rules for 75 days from March 17, 2020 to June 1, 2020, subject to the court's discretion: Coble v Atkin, 2023 ABKB 10 at para 28. [61] A party resisting the dismissal can point to any step in the action by any party, and related to only some but not all defendants, as long there has been a significant advancement of the action as a whole: Flock v Flock, 2017 ABCA 67 at para 17-7; 1499925 Alberta Ltd v NB Developments Ltd, 2023 ABKB 114 at para 57 (and cases cited therein). [62] Whether a step significantly advances the action is determined by a functional, context-sensitive, substance-over-form approach: Rahmani at paras 14 and 22; Flock at paras 17-1 and 17-2; Patil v Cenovus Energy Inc, 2020 ABCA 385 at para 7. [63] A significant advance is one that moves the action forward in an essential or meaningful way, reflecting important or notable progress towards the resolution of an action: Loncikova v Goldstein, 2023 ABCA 358 at para 9; Patil at para 7; Rahmani at para 14; Jacobs v McElhanney Land Surveys Ltd, 2019 ABCA 220 at para 86. This is assessed by viewing the whole picture of what transpired during the relevant period, framed by the real issues in dispute, and viewed through a lens trained on qualitative assessment: Ro-Dar Contracting Ltd v Verbeek Sand & Gravel, 2016 ABCA 123 at para 21. [64] The assessment requires the Court to ask: Has anything that happened in the applicable period increased by a measurable degree the likelihood either the parties or a court would have sufficient information – usually a better idea of the facts that can be proven – and be in a better position to rationally assess the merits of the parties' positions and either settle or adjudicate the action? Are the parties at the end of the applicable period much closer to resolution than they were at the start date? (Loncikova at para 9; Morrison v Galvanic Applied Sciences Inc, 2019 ABCA 207 at para 35; Jacobs at para 86; Weaver v Cherniawsky, 2016 ABCA 152 at para 26.) [65] Answering these questions involves an assessment of the nature, quality, genuineness, and timing of the advancing conduct: Patil at para 7; Rahmani at para 14; Ursa Ventures Ltd v Edmonton (City), 2016 ABCA 135 at para 19; Ro-Dar at para 21. Steps that narrow issues, clarify positions, complete discovery of documents and information, or ascertain relevant facts or law, may significantly advance an action, but outcomes should not be overemphasized: Ro-Dar at para 20; Stylecraft Developments (1984) Ltd v Carscallen LLP, 2023 ABKB 504 at para 13. [66] While courts understand the challenges facing self-represented parties, the bottom line is that self-represented litigants are expected to familiarize themselves with the relevant legal practices and procedures pertaining to their case and to comply with the Rules, including in the context of delay dismissal applications: Owaise v Condominium Corporation 8310969, 2023 ABCA 88 at para 16; Municipal District of Foothills No 31 v Alston, 2023 ABCA 46 at para 3; Morrison at para 27; AF v Alberta, 2020 ABQB 268; Alston v Haywood Securities Inc, 2020 ABQB 107 at para 114. The standards and requirements of rule 4.33 are not relaxed, bent, or ignored for self-represented litigants, as that would be tantamount to having one set of rules for litigants with counsel and a different set for self-represented litigants: Gjergji v Hyatt Mitsubishi, 2017 ABQB 500 at paras 20-21 and 32; Vanmaele Estate at para 32; Lofstrom v Radke, 2020 ABQB 122 at para 93. [67] The onus is on the party making the dismissal application to lead evidence that no significant advance has occurred within the three year period: Taschuk at paras 37-40; Nahal v Gottlieb, 2019 ABQB 650 at para 11. However, while the overall legal or persuasive burden is on the applicant, if the party resisting the application relies on specific matters as significantly advancing an action, they may have an evidential burden to demonstrate or prove how they do so: see, for example, Taschuk at paras 38-40. The general rule is that a party who asserts a proposition of fact has the burden of proving it: Emeric Holdings Inc v Edmonton (City), 2009 ABCA 65 (per Slatter JA, in dissent) at para 43, citing Robins v National Trust Co, 1927 CanLII 469 (UK JCPC), [1927] AC 515 at p 520 (JCPC, Ont). In Diotte v. 2 Cuz'N Trucking Ltd., 2022 ABKB 741, 2022 CarswellAlta 3259 (Applications Judge), Applications Judge Schlosser said: [17] In my view, r 4.33 should be treated in the same fashion as a summary judgment application. By that I mean that the applicant under the rule, having established a prima facie case, then causes the burden to shift to the plaintiff/respondent to show that there was a significant advance, or a standstill, participation, or a suspension period that would permit the action to continue. In Patil v. Cenovus Energy Inc., 2020 ABCA 385, the Court of Appeal set out several principles which relate to R. 4.33, and said: [7] Several legal principles can be discerned from decisions of this Court interpreting r 4.33: • The rule must be applied within the context of the foundational rule (r 1.2) to resolve claims fairly and justly in a timely and cost-effective way. • Plaintiffs bear the responsibility of prosecuting their claims in a timely way: XS Technologies Inc v Veritas DGC Land Ltd, 2016 ABCA 165 at para 7. • Defendants are obliged (pursuant to r 1.2) to not obstruct, stall or delay an action that the plaintiff is advancing: Janstar Homes Ltd v Elbow Valley West Ltd, 2016 ABCA 417 at para 26. • A functional, as opposed to a formalistic, approach is appropriate to determine if a step constitutes a significant advance: Ursa Ventures Ltd v Edmonton (City), 2016 ABCA 135 at para 19. • The functional approach to r 4.33 is context-sensitive: “[C]ases that have considered a particular advance in an action will be useful precedents, but they are not determinative”: Ursa Ventures at paras 19, 23. • A significant advance is one that moves the action forward in an essential way, having regard to the nature, quality, genuineness and timing of the advancing action: Ursa Ventures at para 19; Ro-Dar Contracting Ltd v Verbeek Sand & Gravel Inc., 2016 ABCA 123 at para 21. • Rule 4.33 functions like a limitations period. It only requires one significant advance within the three-year period, not “continuous significant advancement”. Rule 4.33 is not designed to determine what a “reasonably diligent litigant” would do over the course of the three-year period: Ursa Ventures at para 11. • Whether an agreement between counsel constitutes a significant advance is context-dependent. Rule 4.33 was not designed to encourage an “ambush” by one side after the parties had agreed to take a particular step: Turek v Oliver, 2014 ABCA 327 at para 6. • Courts assessing whether an action is a significant advance under r 4.33 should focus on substance, not form. As an example, agreement to participate in a judicial dispute resolution process may not constitute a significant advance if it was merely an agreement to schedule a JDR, which was not carried out: Weaver v Cherniawsky, 2016 ABCA 152 at paras 20-21. [8] Importantly, r 4.33 is “not designed to regulate the efficient prosecution of actions, but rather to prune out actions that have truly died”: Ursa Ventures at para 10. In Derrick Concrete Cutting & Construction Ltd. v. Nexxt Concrete Cutting & Construction Ltd., 2024 ABKB 190, Justice Neilson said: [37] As delineated by the Court of Appeal in Patil, a functional, as opposed to a formalistic, approach is appropriate to determine if a step constitutes a significant advance. The functional approach to Rule 4.33 is context sensitive. A significant advance is one that moves the action forward in an essential way having regard to the nature, quality, genuineness, and timing of the advancing action. 2. Interpretation of Rule 4.33 In Nash v. Snow, 2014 ABQB 355, 2014 CarswellAlta 952, 58 C.P.C. (7th) 126, Madam Justice Topolniski discussed the approach to be adopted in interpreting R. 4.33. At paragraphs 29–35, her Ladyship said: 29 The absence of the words the “last thing” or “step” in Rule 4.33 necessarily modifies the focus of the purposive and contextual assessment. The issue is “advancing” or moving the action forward and what was done in the context of the real issues in dispute. Accordingly, the court must take a macro view of what transpired in the three-year window. That may require some dissection of what happened, and some examination of the dissected parts. As Graesser J. noted in Le v 1055168 Alberta Ltd, the focus is on function, not whether an act fits into a defined category of activities. 30 Put another way, the court must view the whole picture of what transpired in the three-year period, framed by the real issues in dispute, and viewed through a lens trained on a qualitative assessment. This necessarily involves assessing various factors including, but not limited to, the nature, value and quality, genuineness, timing, and in certain circumstances, the outcome of what occurred. 31 This approach does not affect the view that there is no difference between the words “materially advance” (in old Rule 244.1) and “significantly advance”. However, it may affect the applicability of certain pre-November 1, 2013 authorities, particularly those that applied an analysis based on categories rather than functional impact. b. — The End Goal 32 Slatter J.A. commented in Windsor v Canadian Pacific Railway Ltd at para 15 that “the myth of trial should no longer govern civil procedure”. The culture shift called for in Hryniak and echoed in Windsor supports the Plaintiff's contention that the end goal of “significant advancements” under Rule 4.33 is not necessarily trial, but rather resolution. I agree. 33 The Rules employ the term “resolution” but do not define it. In the context of litigation, the word often conjures images of “settlement” (“The reconciliation of conflicting views or parties in regard to a matter; the settlement of a dispute or conflict”: Oxford English Dictionary, online: <www.oed.com>). Similarly, it can bring to mind a “disposition” (“A formal decision, determination, or expression of opinion by a deliberative assembly, committee, court …”: Oxford English Dictionary, online). Both concepts exist on a litigation continuum ranging from abandonment of an action, to complete or partial settlement, to final disposition by ruling of the tribunal. Final dispositions do not flow only from trials; they can take multiple forms ranging from striking of an unmeritorious action, dismissal of a dormant action, summary judgment or dismissal, summary trial, and a full trial. While a full trial may be “a rarity” as Slatter J.A. observed in Windsor v Canadian Pacific Railway Ltd, for some it is nevertheless inevitable. 34 The Rules speak to dispute resolution with or without the court's assistance (Rule 15 (d)). They place responsibility on the parties to manage their dispute, by engaging in good faith participation in alternate dispute resolution (Rule 4.16), and they mandate some form of dispute resolution (or Order waiving it) before a case can be set for trial (Rule 8.4(3)). None of these notions existed until November 1, 2010 when the new Alberta Rules of Court came into force. Their obvious purpose is to promote affordable, timely, and proportionate dispute resolution and to place squarely on litigants' shoulders the responsibility for working towards resolution of their lawsuit without the need for a trial. 35 The change in tenor of the new Rules supports the notion that litigation is no longer about reaching the ultimate goal of trial. Rather, the goal—as stated in Hryniak and Windsor—is to resolve the case by proportionate means when it is just and fair to do so. In St. Jean Estate v. Edmonton (City), 2014 ABQB 47, Topolniski, J. said, at paragraphs 18-19: 18 The current trend is to employ a functional approach to determine if an action moves the litigation forward in a meaningful way considering the nature, value, importance and quality of the action: Phillips v. Sowan, 2007 ABCA 101, 40 CPC (6th) 378; Brar v. Pawa, 2010 ABQB 779, 506 AR 325 (MC); Franchuk v. Schick, 2013 ABQB 532, [2013] A.J. No. 969 at para 12 (MC); Huynh v. The precursor Rule required a “material advance”, while Rule 4.33 tests delay on the absence of a “significant advance”. the quality of the step or thing must be analyzed. Importantly, the Master focused on the pleadings to see what may be relevant to the lawsuit. [Emphasis added.] See also Madore v. In Huynh v. Rosman, 2013 ABQB 218, 2013 CarswellAlta 548, Justice Gates discussed whether the collection of information will significantly advance an action. His Lordship said: [35]… In determining if a thing significantly advanced an action, the court must undertake a functional analysis and determine if the thing moved the litigation closer to trial in a meaningful way. In a case where the thing done is the collection of information, the determination if the litigation was moved closer to trial will depend on a number of factors, including the importance of the information, the extent of the information, the quality of the information, whether the opposing party was aware the information was being gathered, and if the information was ever provided to the opposing party. … [38] The other party's knowledge and/or receipt of the information is, in my view, a very important consideration because the advancement of an action to trial necessarily requires the involvement of both parties. Litigation is an interactive process between opposing parties, each of whom are required to both initiate steps and respond to actions taken by the opposing party. Moreover, litigation is about the exchange of information and positions between and among parties on various factual and legal issues relevant to the action. One party cannot rely solely on its own efforts to allege that they advanced the action when the defendant has no knowledge such work was being done. It is not until the information is actually shared with the other side that the litigation has some prospect of actually moving forward. As stated by Master Hanebury in Schulze v Whitby Business Development Corp at para 30: From a functional perspective, the material advancement of an action involves both parties to the action. While only one may be doing the behind the scenes collection of information that is the “thing” that advances the action, the other party must at least have some knowledge during the five year period that this is occurring for the action to be materially advanced. Justice Gates' comments were quoted with approval by Justice Armstrong in Riehs Estate (Re), 2021 ABQB 821, 2021 CarswellAlta 2589 at paras. 28-29. The Court of Appeal agreed in Loncikova v. Goldstein, 2023 ABCA 358: [10] A survey of Alberta judgments where one party's information and document gathering was put forward as significantly advancing an action shows the courts have considered the importance of the documents, the information in the documents, the relevance and quality of the information, and, importantly, whether the information and documents were provided to the other party. Relevant, valuable information permits a narrowing of issues, agreement on facts or issues, reconsideration of a party's position or possible steps towards settlement, but none of that is possible if the other party has no knowledge of the work done: [citations omitted]. … [12] In any event, the purpose for which the documents were sought is not determinative on its own. As addressed, an important factor is whether the documents, or the document-gathering process, were communicated to the opposing party: see Huynh at para 37, Huerto at para 43, Riehs Estate at para 36, National Home at para 47. In 1499925 Alberta Ltd. v NB Developments Ltd., 2023 ABKB 114, 2023 CarswellAlta 493, Justice Marion concluded that Rule 4.33 still applies to proceedings in which liability has been determined, but the quantum of damages owed has not: [43] An “applicant” under rule 4.33(1)(a) is a “party to an action”. A “party” is also defined in Schedule 1 of the Rules as “a party to an action”. “Action” is not defined under the Rules. However, in Royal Canadian Legion Norwood (Alberta) Branch 178 v Edmonton (City), 1994 ABCA 37 at para 22, the Court of Appeal adopted the definition of action from Halsbury's Laws of England, 4th Edition Vol. 37, para. 17, page 24: ‘Action’ means any civil proceedings commenced by writ or in any other manner prescribed by rules of court. It has a wide signification as including any method prescribed by those rules of invoking the court's jurisdiction for the adjudication or determination of a lis or legal right or claim or any justiciable issue, question or contest arising between two or more persons or affecting the status of one of them. In its natural meaning ‘action’ refers to any proceeding in the nature of a litigation between a plaintiff and a defendant. It includes any civil proceedings in which there is a plaintiff who sues, and a defendant who is sued, in respect of some cause of action, as contrasted with proceedings, such as statutory proceedings which are embraced in the word ‘matter’. [Emphasis added] [44] This passage connotes that an action is a reference to the process by which disputes are brought and resolved before the court. The question is whether or when an action ceases to be an “action” for the purpose of rule 4.33. In my view, this occurs when the claim in the action has been finally determined against a defendant in a judgment such that there is no substantive lis or justiciable issue between the parties on the merits. At that point, the claim or original debt obligation is transformed or merged into, or has been distilled into, a judgment: Mehra; Lightbody v Goldberg, 1997 CanLII 3404 at para 13. At that point, it has been said there is “no longer an action”: Karaha Bodas Company, LLC v Perusahaan Pertambangan Minyak Dan Gas Bumi Negara, 2010 ABQB 172 at para 14, aff'd 2011 ABCA 291 at para 3. …. [46] …However, not every “judgment”, order, or decision of the court gives rise to a merger of the defendant's obligation, or the plaintiff's claim, with the judgment and the effective end of an action or claims within an action. Where there is a remaining substantive step or determination to be made by the court or the parties to resolve a debt claim, there is not a merger of the claim into the judgment: there continues to be an action and parties to the action as contemplated by rule 4.33. …. [50] Allowing a defendant to apply under rule 4.33 where there has been a judgment on liability, but where damages or judgment quantification have not yet been resolved, does not offend policy considerations. In Yaremchuk v Haight, 2001 ABCA 7, the Court of Appeal held that a party that had been noted in default could file an application under former Rule 244.1(1), which was the equivalent of rule 4.33 under the previous rules: Alberta Rules of Court, Alta Reg 390/1968. The Court said, at para 6: “A defendant who has been noted in default is entitled to expect the plaintiff to pursue his claim for damages in a diligent manner in the same way a defendant who has filed a statement of defence has this entitlement.” See also Anstar Enterprises Ltd v Transamerica Life Canada, 2009 ABCA 196 at para 18; Anglin v Resler, 2022 ABKB 737 at para 39; Agriculture Financial Services Corporation v Zaborski, 2013 ABCA 277 at para 18. [51] In my view, the same rationale applies where a court has found a party to be liable, but the quantification of their liability is not yet resolved. In these circumstances, parties should not, for an indeterminate period of time be forced to face the “constant threat, stress and uncertainty” of a pending but unquantified judgment: Canadian Egg at para 13; Angevine v Blue Range Resource Corporation, 2007 ABQB 433 at para 17. At that stage, the policy of removing stalled actions from the “litigation highway” or giving them a boost to get them moving again continues to exist: Recycling Worx Solutions Inc v Hunter, 2023 ABKB 51 at para 50, citing Jacobs v McElhanney Land Surveys Ltd, 2019 ABCA 220 at para 60; Morrison v Galvanic Applied Sciences Inc, 2019 ABCA 20 at para 9; and Transamerica Life Canada v Oakwood Associates Advisory Group Ltd, 2019 ABCA 276. The expeditious resolution of “all aspects of a dispute” is in the interests of the litigants, the civil justice system as a whole and the greater community: Oslanski v Oslanski, 2021 ABCA 68 para 58. 3. “Participating” in a “proceeding”—Rule 4.33(2)(b) Rule 4.33 has often been called the “drop-dead” rule, but subsection 2(b) contains a “zombie” or “resurrection” (depending upon your philosophy) provision. The meaning of Rule 4.33(2)(b) is discussed in CWC Well Services Corp. v. Option Industries Inc., 2019 ABCA 331, 2019 CarswellAlta 1920. The Court of Appeal held that “the present test is set out in the rule …, and does not carry forward key requirements in [Trout Lake Store Inc. v. Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce, 2003 ABCA 259], such as that acquiescence only arises from participation in a ‘material advance’” (paragraph 6). The Court of Appeal said: [7] The appellants argue that to promote certainty and predictability the exception in R. 4.33(2)(b) should be given a fixed and narrow meaning. They argue that the concept of a “significant advance” in the rule should be carried forward into the exception, and that merely signing a litigation plan is not sufficient. Rule 4.33(2)(b), however, noticeably omits the word “significant.” In contrast to predictability, it depends instead on the discretion of the judge, using the phrase “in the opinion of the court”. The rule also does not adopt the common law test for estoppel, which was urged on us by the appellants. The rule must be interpreted on its present wording, not by reference to similar common law tests, or previous cases interpreting rules with different wording, like Trout Lake. [8] The exception in R. 4.33(2)(b) should be interpreted holistically. Its purpose was described in Flock v Flock Estate, 2017 ABCA 67 at para. 17.10, 49 Alta LR (6th) 41 as being “to enshrine in the rules the ability of the Court to dismiss drop dead applications where defendants have actively participated in an action to an extent and degree that could lead a plaintiff to fairly assume that the defendant has waived the delay”. The interpretation of the rule is not necessarily driven by a technical dissection of terms like “proceeding”, “for a purpose”, “to the extent that”, and “participate”: Ro-Dar Contracting Ltd. v Verbeek Sand & Gravel Inc., 2016 ABCA 123 at paras. 15-6, 37 Alta LR (6th) 258. … [11] Whether in the opinion of the Court a continuation of the action is warranted involves an element of discretion. Appellate intervention is not appropriate absent an error of principle or an unreasonable exercise of the discretion. The decisions of the Master and the chambers judge are justified on this record. As Justice Hall said in the decision from which the appeal was dismissed (CWC Well Services Corp. v. Option Industries Inc., 2019 ABQB 108, 2019 CarswellAlta 297) at paragraph 19: “There is no requirement that the defendant's participation, at this point, significantly advances the action. The requirement is that the participation be for a purpose and to the extent, that warrants the [action] proceeding.” 4. Does the Time Between the Date of the Application and the Hearing/Decision Count against the Respondent? In Kehew Construction Ltd. v. Kehewin Cree Nation, 2017 ABQB 763, 2017 CarswellAlta 2611 (Master), the defendant applied for an order striking the action against it because of delay. The application was heard August 29, 2017, and a reserved decision was issued September 18, 2017. The decision held that answers to undertakings which were given on November 5, 2014 significantly advanced the action. After three years passed from November 5, 2014, the defendant again applied for an order striking the claim. The question arose as to whether the time period between the time the application was filed and the time when it was heard should count in R. 4.33 time calculation. The same question was asked about the time period between the time the application was heard and time when the decision was made. The learned Master said: 6 In Trout Lake Store Inc v Canadian Imperial Bank Commerce, 2003 ABCA 259 (an old Rule 244.1 case), Madam Justice Conrad (for the Court) held: In summary, I believe the appropriate approach on a 244.1 application to dismiss is as follows: 1. The proceedings should be examined as at the date of the application to dismiss for want of prosecution pursuant to Rule 244.1. … These steps will avoid the foot race to the courthouse and it will encourage the party seeking to process its claim to proceed in an expeditious manner throughout. At the same time, it will encourage the non-delaying party to act in a timely basis and, at a minimum, to object to any further action taken by the delaying party at the first opportunity. 7 This is sound logic. The time between the date of the application and the time it is heard should not count. Any delay, especially for a special application, is essentially an institutional delay and should not be counted against the Respondent. The time between the date of the application and the time that it is heard counts as a kind of standstill period to be tacked on to the end. 2. — Should the time between the application and the reserved decision count? 8 This time period does not count in the Jordan context for the purpose of 11(b) of the Charter: • R v Manouni, 2017 ABCA 347 at paras 29, 55-56, per Watson JA and paras 71, 84–94 per Slatter JA. • R v Lavoie, 2017 ABQB 66 at paras 38-39, per Belzil J and • R v Kehler, 2001, 2017 NBQB 96 at paras 29–33, 43–80, 95,104. 9 I do not think it should count here. The same conclusion was reached in Ma v. Kwan, 2018 ABQB 852, 2018 CarswellAlta 2315 (Master) at paragraphs 12–14. In that case, the Master Prowse also commented on the effect, if any, of filing a second application under Rule 4.33; [15] Mr. Kwan's first Rule 4.33 application was filed on June 14, 2017 but not heard until October 10, 2018. Mr. Kwan did not move expeditiously to bring his first delay application forward for a hearing. [16] Then five days before hearing the first Rule 4.33 application, Mr. Kwan filed a second Rule 4.33 application, returnable on the same date the first application was to be heard (October 10, 2018). [17] In my view, the concept of institutional delay applies equally to the second Rule 4.33 application. [18] To rule otherwise would allow a defendant to effectively cause an action to be held in abeyance, by filing the first Rule 4.33 application, and then use the delay so caused to justify success on the second Rule 4.33 application. [19] I say “effectively” because a plaintiff could still move forward with an action in light of the pending first Rule 4.33 application, but this would be to invite the plaintiff to effectively waste the plaintiff's legal fees, and the defendant's legal fees, by proceeding with an action which may shortly be struck under the first Rule 4.33 application. [20] Foundational Rule 1.2(1) states that the purpose of the rules is to provide a means by which claims can be resolved in a timely and cost-effective way. [21] Pressuring litigants to carry on with an action while a dismissal delay application is pending is not a cost-effective interpretation of Rule 4.33. [22] Of course the parties, or the Court on the application on one of the parties, might well decide to carry on with the merits of the lawsuit notwithstanding a pending delay dismissal application. However, the litigants should not effectively be forced to carry on pending a dismissal hearing by interpreting Rule 4.33 so as to allow a party to bring a second delay dismissal application and count, as delay, the period of institutional delay caused by awaiting the hearing of the first application. [23] Accordingly I also dismiss Mr. Kwan's second Rule 4.33 application. Master Prowse's decision was appealed [see: 2019 ABQB 89]. Justice Poelman dismissed the appeal, and said: [22] Presumptively, the filing of a dismissal for long delay application crystalizes the rights of parties as the date of filing. The relevant period of delay is determined by looking back from the date the application was filed, not heard: Flock v Flock Estate, 2017 ABCA 67 (CanLII), 49 Alta. L.R. (6th) 41, para 17(8) leave to appeal to SCC refused, 37552 (19 October 2017). In the usual course, there should be no further steps in the action until the dismissal application has been decided: Riviera Developments Inc. v Midd Financial Corp., 2002 ABQB 853 (CanLII), 325 A.R. 48, para 39. That is implicitly recognized by rule 4.33(2), which provides that mandatory dismissal after three years of delay will not occur if the defendant, having made the application, participates in other proceedings “for a purpose and to the extent that, in the opinion of the Court, warrants the action continuing.” The policy for this exception comes from Trout Lake Store Inc. v Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce, 2003 ABCA 259 (CanLII), 31 Alta. L.R. (4th) 243, which expressed a concern about a defendant acquiescing in the delay: paras 28, 29 and 33. Trout Lake also recognized “some obligation on the defending party to make its application to dismiss on a timely basis”: para 29. [23] It follows, in my view, that presumptively a second application to dismiss for long delay cannot make use of the period after filing of the first application as part of the delay. Doing so would encourage gamesmanship: filing second applications to improve prospects of success by lengthening the period of delay since various possible, arguable steps had been in the action. Or, as observed by Prowse M. (para 19), Mr. Ma may have felt compelled to proceed with his oppression application after the first delay application was filed, in an effort to significantly advance his application during the period after filing—because of the possibility of the second application being filed before the first is heard. That is not a reasonable use of either party's resources, as noted by Prowse M.: para 21. [24] Thus, the courts have long contemplated that there can be no further steps until the dismissal application has been heard: Riviera, para 39. That need not be a long time, in the scheme of an action that is the subject of a dismissal application. Further, it is assumed that a party complaining of delay will prosecute its application to dismiss on a timely basis. Here, it cannot tenably be suggested that Mr. Kwan pursued his first application with alacrity. Prowse M. observed that “Mr. Kwan did not move expeditiously to bring his first delay application forward for a hearing”: para 15. In Xpress Lube & Car Wash Ltd. v. Gill, 2019 ABQB 898, 2019 CarswellAlta 2510, Justice Eamon said: [101] Master Robertson QC reasoned (at para 68) that the period of delay must be determined by looking back from the date the applications were filed, not heard, citing Ma v Kwan, 2019 ABQB 89 at para 22. Three years had not elapsed from October 23, 2015 until the date the applications were filed. Therefore, he refused to dismiss the Actions under Rule 4.33. … [103] Case law supports Master Robertson's conclusion that time is measured from the filing date of the dismissal application. See Flock v Flock Estate, 2017 ABCA 67 at para 17(8), and numerous authorities in this Court, including Ma v Kwan, Kirkness v Emberley, 2019 ABQB 159 at para 24 and the numerous authorities cited in footnote 9 of the Kirkness decision. Flock is quite specific about the matter: … In addition to the principles affirmed in Ro-Dar[Consulting Ltd v Verbeek Sand & Gravel Inc, 2016 ABCA 123] the following additional principles relating to the interpretation of rule 4.33 maintain effect: … 8. The relevant period of delay must be determined by looking back from the date the application was filed, not heard: Steparyk v Alberta, 2014 ABQB 367 (CanLII) at para 5. (Italics in original) 5. Three years must have passed In Covey v. Devon Canada Corporation, 2020 ABCA 445, 2020 CarswellAlta 2400, the Court said: [15] The respondent's argument is essentially this: under r 4.33, the court “must dismiss” the action if “3 or more years have passed without a significant advance”. It does not say “more than 3 years” or that the court must dismiss the action if there is no significant advance “within 3 years” If r 4.33 said either of those things, service of the affidavit of records on May 12, 2018 would have been within the required period. However, r 4.33 sets the drop-dead date, on which the action is out of time, at three years from the last significant advance; therefore, the respondent argues, the significant advance must take place earlier than three years since the last significant advance. The respondent acknowledges that the jurisprudence contains some passing references to the deadline being less than three years, but that no court has addressed the issue head on: see Ursa at para 11 referring to “prior to the expiration of three years” or Maurice v Matchett, 2016 ABQB 704 at para 49 referring to “3 years less a day”. [16] We disagree with the respondent's position. Under r 4.33, the three years have to “have passed”. … 6. Count forward from last uncontroversial significant advance In Rahmani v. 959630 Alberta Ltd., 2021 ABCA 110, 2021 CarswellAlta 639, the Court said: [16] First, it is necessary to address the rules for calculating time. When counting time, one counts forward from the date of the last uncontroversial significant advance, not backward from the date on which the r 4.33 application was filed. This is clear from the wording of r 4.33(2); “if three or more years have passed without a significant advance in an action” (emphasis added). The time has to be measured from a date and so must be measured from the last significant advance: Trout Lake Store Inc v Canadian Bank of Imperial Commerce, 2003 ABCA 259 at paras 25–33; Barath v Schloss, 2015 ABQB 332 at para 9. In this case, the last uncontroversial significant advance was the provision of answers to undertakings on July 8, 2014. [17] When counting time following a significant advance, the count stops on the date the r 4.33 application was filed, not the date that the application was heard. The time between the application being filed and the application being heard does not count against the respondent: Flock v Flock Estate, 2017 ABCA 67 at para 17(8); Ma v Kwan, 2018 ABQB 852 at paras 11–14. Therefore, the relevant window of time in this case is July 8, 2014 to July 13, 2018, when the application to dismiss for long delay was filed. Was there a three year period between these dates without any significant advance in the action? 7. Rule is Mandatory In Wilson (Next Friend of) v. Aspen View Regional School, Division No. 19, 2014 ABQB 741, 2014 CarswellAlta 2232, Madam Justice Goss said, at paragraph 23: [23] The case law is clear to the effect that Rule 4.33(1) is mandatory. Subject to the parties agreeing to the delay or another of the exceptions listed, a court has no discretion to save a dormant action: Nash v Snow, 2014 ABQB 355 (CanLII) at para 12, 58 CPC (7th) 126, citing Morasch and Trout Lake Store Inc v Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce, 2003 ABCA 259 (CanLII), 330 AR 379. The Rule promotes certainty and expeditious litigation. The requirement to dismiss languishing litigation is also consistent with Rule 1.2(1) which declares that the purpose of the rules is to provide a means by which claims can be fairly and justly resolved in or by a court process in a timely and cost-effective way: Nash, paras 19-20. In Chak v. Sun Media Corporation, 2017 ABQB 614, 2017 CarswellAlta 1842 (Master), Master Schlosser said: 9 Rule 4.33 is a bright-line rule. It has only to do with timing, not merits. A decision to dismiss for delay has nothing to do with the strength of Mr. Chak's claim and, in particular, nothing to do with whether what Mr. Levant said (and the Defendants published) was defamatory. 8. Rule 4.33 and the effect of the Interpretation Act. In In Droog v. Hamilton, 2024 ABKB 243, the three-year period prescribed by R. 4.33 presumptively expired on Saturday, May 22, 2021. The plaintiff served, by email, defendants’ counsel with an Affidavit of Records on Tuesday, May 25, 2021. Monday, the 24th of May was a statutory holiday: Victoria Day. The plaintiff submitted that the service of the Affidavit of Records (which in the view of the court constituted, in this particular lawsuit, an act which significantly advanced the action) was, in law, effected within the 3 years because of section 22(2) of the Interpretation Act (Alberta) which states: “If in an enactment the time limited for registration or filing of an instrument, or for the doing of anything, expires or falls on a day on which the office or place in which the instrument or thing is required to be registered, filed or done is not open during its regular hours of business, the instrument or thing may be registered, filed or done on the day next following on which the office or place is open.” Justice C. M. Jones held that section 22(2) of the Interpretation Act does apply to Rule 4.33. Justice Jones said: [20] I note that Rule 4.33 itself does not specify that a significant advance must occur at a specified place. This makes sense given that different steps can and sometimes must occur at different places. For example, as the Applications Judge stated, filing a Statement of Claim must be done at the courthouse or its electronic repository. Under the Alberta Business Corporations Act, service on a corporation must be made at its registered office. In contrast, some significant advances do not have to occur at legislatively prescribed locations; for example, parties could enter into a settlement agreement at a local pub. [21] Therefore, I am of the view that s 22(2) of the Interpretation Act can be applied to Rule 4.33 by considering the purported significant advance and assessing whether that particular act is, by its nature, required (by legislation, custom or agreement) to be done at a specific location. If so, and if the particular location was closed on the date in question, there is a basis to extend the deadline pursuant to s. 22(2). Even so, Justice Jones found that the legislation did not, in this case, assist the plaintiff: [22] In this case, the Respondents provided an address for service at the offices of their counsel. The documents filed by the Respondents give counsel’s business address, the names of the specific lawyers, and the telephone and fax numbers, but no email address. There is no dispute that email service was not specifically agreed to. Rule 11.15 provides that service of a non-commencement document on lawyers providing an address for service is effective on the date the document is “left:. at that address”. [23] I accept that the Appellants could not have effected service on the Presumptive Expiry Date by physically leaving the AoR at Respondents’ counsel’s office because the office was not open to accept it. However, the Respondents assert in their brief that service could have been effected by fax on that date. I agree. On a strict reading of s 22(2) of the Interpretation Act, I am not satisfied it is correct to say that counsel’s offices were not “open” on the Presumptive Expiry Date. The concept of “regular business hours” has no meaning in respect of fax service. Because the Respondents had provided counsel’s fax number as part of their address for service, I find that it was not necessary for counsel’s office to be open for fax service to be effected. Similarly, if the parties had agreed to email service, I find that this too could have been effected on the Presumptive Expiry Date notwithstanding that counsel’s office was not physically open. [24] Given that one method of service was not available to the Appellants on the Presumptive Expiry Date but others were, how is s 22(2) of the Interpretation Act to be interpreted? I note that the statute does not expressly require that there be no other method of doing the thing in question before its relieving provisions apply. It does not expressly exclude relief in circumstances where the thing that had to be done could have been done in another manner that would obviate the need for such relief. I am also mindful that Rule 11.27 allows relief for defects in service. [25] However, I also note that Rule 4.33 is mandatory. The Court takes a dim view of delay and the Rules do not give the Court discretion where long delay is found. Accordingly, while I have discretion under Rule 11.27, I do not think it appropriate to exercise that discretion in this context. I would be frustrating the spirit and intent of Rule 4.33, and arguably the foundational Rules, by giving the Appellants the requested relief. [26] Consequently, I agree with the Applications Judge that s 22(2) of the Interpretation Act does not assist the Appellants. The three-year period contemplated by Rule 4.33 expired without a significant advance in the Action and, accordingly, the Appellants’ Action is hereby struck. 9. Agreement to the delay In Brian W. Conway Professional Corp. v. River Rock Lodge Corp., 2015 ABQB 359, [appeal dismissed: 2015 ABCA 404] Justice Campbell said: 39 Rule 4.33(1)(a) of the Rules permits parties to expressly agree to delay proceeding with an action and thereby restrict the application of Rule 4.33(1) that could otherwise result in the dismissal of an action for long delay. 40 Jurisprudence has established that the essential features of an express agreement or standstill agreement referred to in Rule 4.33 are: (i) that the parties' intention must be clear and not based on intent or inference; (ii) that the agreement cannot be implied from conduct; and, (iii) at the very least, there must be evidence of the basic elements of an agreement such as the identity of the parties to the contract, when the agreement began and its essential terms: Bugg v Beau Canada Exploration Ltd, 2006 ABCA 201 at paras 8-9; Sucker Creek First Nation v Canada (Attorney General), 2013 ABQB 199 (“Sucker Creek”) at paras 23–26. A standstill agreement can be found in correspondence exchanged among counsel: Sucker Creek at para 36; Sinnott v Canadian Pacific Railway, 2010 ABQB 185 at para 8. 41 However, the case law reminds us that there is a distinction to keep in mind. While an express or standstill agreement does not have to be completely in writing, such an agreement must clearly be demonstrated on the evidence provided, without recourse to conduct, intent or inference. That said, there is no requirement for the parties to reference the “drop dead” date or how the agreement would impact the now three-year time period in Rule 4.33, because the court can determine such facts by inference from the words used and the circumstances: Sucker Creek at paras 34-35. Also see the annotations under Rule 4.32. 10. What is a “proceeding”? In Krieter v. Alberta, 2014 ABQB 349, 2014 CarswellAlta 935 (Master), Master Hanebury said, at paragraphs 55-56: 55 The term “proceeding” is not defined in the Rules of Court. 56 While the term “proceeding” can equate to a hearing or meeting, its broader definition includes “all steps in an action from its commencement to the rendering of a decision and the execution of judgment”: Dawe v. Evans, 2009 ABQB 724, paragraph 30. In the context of rule 4.33(1) this broader definition is clearly more applicable. The learned Master then concluded that a Notice to Admit is a “proceeding”: 57 A Notice to Admit is a step in an action, albeit not a mandatory step. In my view, in the context of the rule, a Notice to Admit comes within the definition of “proceeding”. 11. Which Party Must Significantly Advance The Action? In Carter v. Sears Canada Inc., 2011 ABQB 732, 2011 CarswellAlta 2261, 529 A.R. 394, the Plaintiff submitted the foundational Rules now compel “the parties to jointly and individually move the action forward in a fair and just manner and in a timely and cost effective way” and that the Defendant has “an obligation to move the matter forward just as the Plaintiff does.” Justice Hall disagreed. At paragraph 30, his Lordship said: 30 I do not accept that to be the intention of the new Rules of Court. The specific obligations of each party are set out therein, and each party must meet those specific obligations. However, when it comes to prosecuting a claim, the ultimate responsibility still remains with the party making the claim to ensure that it moves forward in such a manner that Rules 4.33 and 15.4 are not violated. The Plaintiff has failed to meet that seminal obligation in this case, either under the old Rules or the new. 12. Was The Action Significantly Advanced? Use A Functional Approach In Alston v. Haywood Securities Inc., 2020 ABQB 107, 2020 CarswellAlta 288, Justice Eamon said: [50] Generally, “[a]“significant advance” in an action is something that “… moves the lawsuit forward in an essential way considering its nature, value, importance and quality … The focus is on substance and effect, not form …”: Ursa Ventures Ltd v Edmonton (City), 2016 ABCA 135 at para 19.” (Arbeau at para 11). The genuineness and the timing of the step are also relevant (Weaver v Cherniawsky, 2016 ABCA 152, at paras 17-18). [51] The focus is on the substance of the step taken and its effect on the litigation, rather than on its form (Weaver at para 18). The test is whether there was a significant advance in the action, not whether unaccepted proposals or attempted procedures could have resulted in a significant advance in other circumstances (Delver v Gladue, 2019 ABCA 54 at para 13). Steps “that serve to narrow the issues, complete the discovery of documents and information, or clarify the positions of the parties might well significantly advance the action” (Ro-Dar Contracting Ltd v Verbeek Sand & Gravel Inc, 2016 ABCA 123 at para 20). Outcomes are also relevant in appropriate cases, but the outcome of a step should not be overemphasized (Sutherland v Brown, 2018 ABCA 123 at para 11). [52] The plaintiff bears the ultimate responsibility to move their action forward (XS Technologies Inc v Veritas DGC Land Ltd, 2016 ABCA 165 at para 7). Defence delay alone does not preclude the time limitation from running. There is no duty on an applying party to expressly advise a responding party that it does not acquiesce to delay (Flock at para 24). There must be something more, such as an express agreement to suspend or waive the passage of time; defence conduct that purposely obstructs, stalls or delays the action; or defence participation that would make it unjust to dismiss the action such as lulling the plaintiff into believing the defence would not object to delay. [53] Illustrative examples of the Alberta Courts' application of these principles include: (a) An unsuccessful proposal to schedule a trial of an issue was found not to have significantly advanced an action (Delver at para 15). (b) A summary judgment application, by itself, is not a significant advance (Jacobs v McElhanney Land Surveys Ltd, 2019 ABCA 220). (c) An application that is dismissed might be characterized as a significant advance factually and legally, if the application procedures advanced the parties' understanding of the facts that may be proven and how the law applies to the facts (Jacobs at paras 117-118). (d) A response to an undertaking is generally a thing that advances an action, unless it is perfunctory or designed to thwart, rather than advance, resolution of the litigation (Ravvin Holdings Ltd v Ghitter, 2008 ABCA 208 at paras 23–30; see also XS Technologies at para 25). (e) A response to a notice to admit might advance an action depending on the circumstances (Jacobs at paras 127-128). (f) A settlement proposal that provided important new information, or narrowed the issues or clarified the parties' positions might significantly advance the action (Delver at paras 12–14). (g) Correspondence among counsel requesting dates for various procedural steps typically do not assist in narrowing the factual or legal issues (Jacobs at paras 131–134). In Forest Resource Improvement Assn. of Alberta v. Moore, 2015 ABQB 588, the Plaintiff submitted that its filing of a Supplemental Affidavit of Records significantly advanced its lawsuit. Justice Little disagreed on the basis that the additional documents disclosed in the Supplemental Affidavit of Records were neither relevant nor material. Justice Little said: 29 FRIAA argues that the filing of the supplemental affidavit of records in the Ringwald action on January 11, 2011 significantly advanced the action within three years of the November 1, 2013 drop dead date. Apex Land Corporation, 2009 ABQB 12, Master Hanebury addressed whether filing an affidavit of records advanced the action. She concluded that there is an obligation to keep an affidavit of records “evergreen,” and therefore filing a supplemental affidavit of records may significantly advance the action. The Court, however, must functionally examine the supplementary affidavit to ascertain whether it contains new documents “and if those documents are in fact documents that materially advance the action” (at para 33, emphasis added). Further, she noted that if the documents materially advanced the action, the reason for filing the supplemental record must be examined to avoid to avoid a foot race to the court. The question in that case was whether the documents were filed at the request of the other party or voluntarily. 31 Lamont Highway Service Lt. v Scraba, 1999 ABQB 1057 (at para 13) and Ro-Dar Contracting Ltd. Verbeek Sand & Gravel Inc, 2015 ABQB 300 (at para 119), stand for the proposition that the supplemental affidavit must be something more than a “housekeeping step” that merely formalized the earlier disclosure of documents or included those that were already in the possession of the defendant. 32“A review must be made of the value of the document in the litigation and whether it moved the matter closer to resolution” (Huynh v. Rosman, 2013 ABQB 218, Gates J at para 36). But because they were copies of permits issued to him, presumably he had already seen them. Also, he had already pleaded that he did not have to pay by reason of a limitations argument. For these reasons, I cannot find that they were relevant or material. As such, the disclosure of these documents did not significantly advance the action or bring the matter closer to resolution. (8th) 33, the Court said: 10 With respect to the balance of the appeal, the 2013 amendments to the Alberta Rules of Court and case law following Hryniak v Mauldin, 2014 SCC 7, [2014] 1 SCR 87 adopt a functional approach towards the resolution of litigation that is not limited to trial in recognition that “a culture shift is required in order to create an environment promoting timely and affordable access to the civil justice system”: para 2. 11 The determination of whether there has been a significant advance towards resolution of an action must be viewed in this context: “steps that serve to narrow the issues, complete the discovery of documents and information, or clarify the positions of the parties might well significantly advance the action. ‘Outcomes’ should not be overemphasized”: Ro-Dar at para 20. This generated a large body of inscrutable law about what was a “step” and what was “not a step”. (b) Before 1994, R. 244 was the general delay rule that provided that an action could be dismissed at any time if prejudice was shown. That was the precursor to R. 4.31. (c) In 1994 the delay rules were completely revised and R. 244.1, the first “drop dead” rule, was introduced. It provided for mandatory dismissal of an action “where 5 or more years have expired from the time that the last thing was done in an action that materially advances the action”. In an attempt to get away from the law on what was a “step”, the rule was written to refer to a “thing that materially advances the action”. In this context “thing” was meant in the sense of “something” or “anything”. (e) The rule was then amended again in 2013, removing all references to either “steps” or “things”, and merely requiring a “significant advance in the action”. An awareness of the legislative history of the rule is helpful in its interpretation. (3d) 386 (Q.B.); [additional reasons at (1998) 67 Alta. L.R. (3d) 240 (Q.B.)], Lee J. agreed that R. 244.1 does not apply to the Crown. He noted that although the general rule is that the Crown is immune from limitation periods unless there is specific legislation to the contrary, there is a “necessary implication” exception to the general rule. At pp. 397-98, His Lordship said: The right of the Crown to proceed with an action cannot be barred by any limitation periods whether contained in the Limitations of Actions Act or in the Rules of Court, unless there is specific legislation to the contrary … The Crown prerogative also applies to agents or trustees of the Crown… In order for a limitation period to bind the Crown or its agents, the enactment when considered in context must “mention or refer” to the Crown in a manner clearly conveying the intention to bind the Crown. 37. The Rule Can Apply To Divorce Actions In Danis-Sim v. Sim, 2024 ABCA 297, affirmed 2023 ABKB 637, the Court addressed the question of whether Rule 4.33 gives a judge a discretion to not strike an action in cases when the absence of an applicable limitation date would allow the action to be recommenced. In Danis-Sim v. Sim, supra, a Divorce Judgment and Corollary Relief Order was granted in 2008, and it provided that the wife was ordered to pay child support to the husband who had been granted sole custody of the three children of the marriage. In 2017, the husband registered the Divorce Judgment and Corollary Relief Order with the Maintenance Enforcement Program claiming arrears of $42,000. The wife then filed an application “seeking an order reducing child support arrears to $0.” In August 2017, an interim order was granted reducing the wife's child support arrears to $11,150, and setting out both payments to be made to address the arrears and setting out future child support payments. The wife made the payments required of her by the interim order. In May 2022, the husband filed an application “for an order dismissing [the wife's] June 2017 child support arrears application and striking the August 2017 interim order.” The husband relied on Rule 4.33 and submitted that “more than three years had passed without a significant advance in the application and that the relief he sought ‘must’ therefore be granted.” The learned Chambers Judge noted that “the delay rules apply to divorce and other family law proceedings”, but “noted that dismissing the [wife's] child support arrears application for long delay would not prevent the respondent from initiating a new application if she chose to do so. Consequently, dismissing the application ‘would serve no purpose and lead to needless cost and delay’”. The Court of Appeal ultimately dismissed the appeal because it held that “the language of rule 4.33 limits its application to dismissing ‘actions’ for long delay. It is not designed for managing applications brought by one or another of the parties within an action, and in no event can it be used to reverse existing orders”: paragraph 25. The Court said at paragraph 31: “…we cannot collapse the distinction drawn between actions and applications in rule 4.33 to make the mandatory dismissal provision available for the [husband's] purposes.” However, the Court took the opportunity to specifically state that there existed no discretion in the learned chambers judge to dismiss the application on the ground that granting it would “serve no purpose” because the wife could have initiated a new application. The Court of Appeal said: [19] As the chambers judge observed, beginning with Wittenburg v Wittenburg, 2003 ABQB 154, several Alberta decisions have questioned the utility of rule 4.33 (and former rule 244.1[2]) in the family law context because dismissing an action for long delay when a plaintiff can simply restart it tends to invite nothing but unnecessary cost and further delay: see for e.g., as cited by the chambers judge, Boland v Carew, 2018 ABQB 317 (Boland QB), aff'd Boland CA; Soriano v Bacalla, 2021 ABQB 195; Blume v Blume, 2022 ABQB 539; see also, Thompson v Thompson, 2007 ABQB 715; Pilon v Lavoie, 2024 ABKB 177. What the chambers judge appears to have missed is none of these cases stand for the proposition she made: that in the context of an action under the Divorce Act, an application under rule 4.33 may be dismissed as serving no purpose in the absence of an applicable limitation period. [20] In Wittenburg, Thompson and Pilon, the court commented on the undesirable consequences of dismissal for delay where no limitation deadline would prevent a new action for the same relief, but in each case the action was struck. [21] In Boland QB, the chambers judge referred to Wittenburg's discussion about the utility of dismissing an action under the Divorce Act for delay when there is no limitation period preventing another action but found the applicant had “continued to participate in the action and otherwise acquiesced in the delay”: at para 21. This engaged one of the two exceptions under rule 4.33(2). This Court dismissed the appeal but arrived at the result differently. It characterized the applicant's continued participation – which included negotiating and honoring a settlement agreement in relation to child support before he unilaterally stopped paying – as a significant advance in the action. The Court noted at paragraphs 14 and 17 of Boland CA that rule 4.33: … should not be applied in a manner so as to discourage litigants from settling aspects of their ongoing disputes, even where the entire dispute is not settled, for fear that three years later the other party will be able to defeat the resolution of ongoing claims simply by bringing an application to dismiss. … We observe that to endorse a payor's unilateral decision to stop making the agreed-upon child support payments and to then apply to strike the payee's underlying action for same, arguing that no proceedings had been taken for more than 3 years, would be to permit the payor parent to set a trap to force the payee to go to the expense of recommencing and prosecuting child support; if she could not afford or was otherwise unable to take that step, the payor could practically be absolved from further payment and his child deprived of the benefits of that support. … [22] The Court also observed, in obiter, that if the application to dismiss for delay was granted, there was nothing to prevent the respondent from recommencing her action for divorce and bringing a new application to pursue her claims for divorce and child support, possibly including an action on the parties' earlier settlement agreement. It was not a circumstance in which the applicant could benefit from the lapse of any statutory limitation period. The reasons in Boland CA do not say that the mandatory nature of rule 4.33 can be relaxed in the family law context, in the discretion of the court, when no limitation period applies. [23] In both Soriano and Blume, the court refused to dismiss claims (one for spousal support and the other for matrimonial property where no divorce judgment had been obtained) for delay but not strictly on the basis that the court had discretion to disregard the mandatory language of rule 4.33 where a limitation period has yet to lapse. [24] While the absence of an applicable limitation period may be considered under rule 4.31, which affords the court discretion to dismiss all or any part of a claim if there is delay that has resulted in significant prejudice to a party, the plain language of rule 4.33 affords judges no such discretion. The chambers judge erred to the extent she determined otherwise. 38. Rule 4.33 applies to “actions” and not “applications” In Danis-Sim v. Sim, 2024 ABCA 297, the Court said: [30] Rule 4.33(2) consistently refers to an “action” being dismissed. The term “application” is not used, except in rule 4.33(2)(b) which sets out one of the two exceptions to dismissing an action for long delay as: “an application has been filed or proceedings have been taken since the delay and the applicant has participated in them for a purpose and to the extent that, in the opinion of the Court, warrants the action continuing.” The exception distinguishes an “action” from an “application” or “proceedings” in the context of the drop-dead rule and reinforces that rule 4.33 is intended to apply to actions and not applications brought, or proceedings taken, within them.

A Brief Overview In Abou Shaaban v.

Baljak, 2024 ABKB 28, additional reasons 2024 ABKB 125, Justice Marion provided this useful summary of the law: [60] The relevant period of delay must be determined by starting with the last uncontroversial significant advance up to the date the dismissal application was filed (not the date it was heard): Rahmani v 959630 Alberta Ltd, 2021 ABCA 110 at paras 16-17
Vanmaele Estate (Re), 2023 ABKB 456 at para 21
Taschuk v Taschuk, 2022 ABKB 786 at para 13
Babiuk v Heap, 2023 ABKB 410 at para 48.
A question to be asked is: “was there a three year period between these dates without any significant advance in the action?”: Rahmani at para 17.

If the relevant period of delay includes March 17, 2020 to June 1, 2020, then Ministerial Order 27/2020 must be considered, as it suspended the operation of time limits under the Rules for 75 days from March 17, 2020 to June 1, 2020, subject to the court's discretion: Coble v Atkin, 2023 ABKB 10 at para 28.

[61] A party resisting the dismissal can point to any step in the action by any party, and related to only some but not all defendants, as long there has been a significant advancement of the action as a whole: Flock v Flock, 2017 ABCA 67 at para 17-7; 1499925 Alberta Ltd v NB Developments Ltd, 2023 ABKB 114 at para 57 (and cases cited therein).
[62] Whether a step significantly advances the action is determined by a functional, context-sensitive, substance-over-form approach: Rahmani at paras 14 and 22
Flock at paras 17-1 and 17-2
Patil v Cenovus Energy Inc, 2020 ABCA 385 at para 7.

[63] A significant advance is one that moves the action forward in an essential or meaningful way, reflecting important or notable progress towards the resolution of an action: Loncikova v Goldstein, 2023 ABCA 358 at para 9
Patil at para 7
Rahmani at para 14
Jacobs v McElhanney Land Surveys Ltd, 2019 ABCA 220 at para 86.

This is assessed by viewing the whole picture of what transpired during the relevant period, framed by the real issues in dispute, and viewed through a lens trained on qualitative assessment: Ro-Dar Contracting Ltd v Verbeek Sand & Gravel, 2016 ABCA 123 at para 21.

[64] The assessment requires the Court to ask: Has anything that happened in the applicable period increased by a measurable degree the likelihood either the parties or a court would have sufficient information – usually a better idea of the facts that can be proven – and be in a better position to rationally assess the merits of the parties' positions and either settle or adjudicate the action?
Are the parties at the end of the applicable period much closer to resolution than they were at the start date?
(Loncikova at para 9
Morrison v Galvanic Applied Sciences Inc, 2019 ABCA 207 at para 35
Jacobs at para 86
Weaver v Cherniawsky, 2016 ABCA 152 at para 26.) [65] Answering these questions involves an assessment of the nature, quality, genuineness, and timing of the advancing conduct: Patil at para 7
Rahmani at para 14
Ursa Ventures Ltd v Edmonton (City), 2016 ABCA 135 at para 19
Ro-Dar at para 21.

Steps that narrow issues, clarify positions, complete discovery of documents and information, or ascertain relevant facts or law, may significantly advance an action, but outcomes should not be overemphasized: Ro-Dar at para 20
Stylecraft Developments
(1984) Ltd v Carscallen LLP, 2023 ABKB 504 at para 13.

[66] While courts understand the challenges facing self-represented parties, the bottom line is that self-represented litigants are expected to familiarize themselves with the relevant legal practices and procedures pertaining to their case and to comply with the Rules, including in the context of delay dismissal applications: Owaise v Condominium Corporation 8310969, 2023 ABCA 88 at para 16
Municipal District of Foothills No 31 v Alston, 2023 ABCA 46 at para 3
Morrison at para 27
AF v Alberta, 2020 ABQB 268
Alston v Haywood Securities Inc, 2020 ABQB 107 at para 114.

The standards and requirements of rule 4.33 are not relaxed, bent, or ignored for self-represented litigants, as that would be tantamount to having one set of rules for litigants with counsel and a different set for self-represented litigants: Gjergji v Hyatt Mitsubishi, 2017 ABQB 500 at paras 20-21 and 32
Vanmaele Estate at para 32
Lofstrom v Radke, 2020 ABQB 122 at para 93.

[67] The onus is on the party making the dismissal application to lead evidence that no significant advance has occurred within the three year period: Taschuk at paras 37-40; Nahal v Gottlieb, 2019 ABQB 650 at para 11.

However, while the overall legal or persuasive burden is on the applicant, if the party resisting the application relies on specific matters as significantly advancing an action, they may have an evidential burden to demonstrate or prove how they do so: see, for example, Taschuk at paras 38-40.

The general rule is that a party who asserts a proposition of fact has the burden of proving it: Emeric Holdings Inc v Edmonton (City), 2009 ABCA 65 (per Slatter JA, in dissent) at para 43, citing Robins v National Trust Co, 1927 CanLII 469 (UK JCPC), [1927] AC 515 at p 520 (JCPC, Ont).
In Diotte v.

2 Cuz'N Trucking Ltd., 2022 ABKB 741, 2022 CarswellAlta 3259 (Applications Judge), Applications Judge Schlosser said: [17] In my view, r 4.33 should be treated in the same fashion as a summary judgment application.

By that I mean that the applicant under the rule, having established a prima facie case, then causes the burden to shift to the plaintiff/respondent to show that there was a significant advance, or a standstill, participation, or a suspension period that would permit the action to continue.
In Patil v.
Cenovus Energy Inc., 2020 ABCA 385, the Court of Appeal set out several principles which relate to R.

4.33, and said: [7] Several legal principles can be discerned from decisions of this Court interpreting r 4.33: • The rule must be applied within the context of the foundational rule (r 1.2) to resolve claims fairly and justly in a timely and cost-effective way. • Plaintiffs bear the responsibility of prosecuting their claims in a timely way: XS Technologies Inc v Veritas DGC Land Ltd, 2016 ABCA 165 at para 7. • Defendants are obliged (pursuant to r 1.2) to not obstruct, stall or delay an action that the plaintiff is advancing: Janstar Homes Ltd v Elbow Valley West Ltd, 2016 ABCA 417 at para 26. • A functional, as opposed to a formalistic, approach is appropriate to determine if a step constitutes a significant advance: Ursa Ventures Ltd v Edmonton (City), 2016 ABCA 135 at para 19. • The functional approach to r 4.33 is context-sensitive: “[C]ases that have considered a particular advance in an action will be useful precedents, but they are not determinative”: Ursa Ventures at paras 19, 23. • A significant advance is one that moves the action forward in an essential way, having regard to the nature, quality, genuineness and timing of the advancing action: Ursa Ventures at para 19
Ro-Dar Contracting Ltd v Verbeek Sand & Gravel Inc., 2016 ABCA 123 at para 21. • Rule 4.33 functions like a limitations period.
It only requires one significant advance within the three-year period, not “continuous significant advancement”.

Rule 4.33 is not designed to determine what a “reasonably diligent litigant” would do over the course of the three-year period: Ursa Ventures at para 11. • Whether an agreement between counsel constitutes a significant advance is context-dependent.

Rule 4.33 was not designed to encourage an “ambush” by one side after the parties had agreed to take a particular step: Turek v Oliver, 2014 ABCA 327 at para 6. • Courts assessing whether an action is a significant advance under r 4.33 should focus on substance, not form.

As an example, agreement to participate in a judicial dispute resolution process may not constitute a significant advance if it was merely an agreement to schedule a JDR, which was not carried out: Weaver v Cherniawsky, 2016 ABCA 152 at paras 20-21.
[8] Importantly, r 4.33 is “not designed to regulate the efficient prosecution of actions, but rather to prune out actions that have truly died”: Ursa Ventures at para 10.
In Derrick Concrete Cutting & Construction Ltd. v.

Nexxt Concrete Cutting & Construction Ltd., 2024 ABKB 190, Justice Neilson said: [37] As delineated by the Court of Appeal in Patil, a functional, as opposed to a formalistic, approach is appropriate to determine if a step constitutes a significant advance.
The functional approach to Rule 4.33 is context sensitive.
A significant advance is one that moves the action forward in an essential way having regard to the nature, quality, genuineness, and timing of the advancing action.
Interpretation of Rule 4.33 In Nash v.
Snow, 2014 ABQB 355, 2014 CarswellAlta 952, 58 C.P.C.
(7th) 126, Madam Justice Topolniski discussed the approach to be adopted in interpreting R.
At paragraphs 29–35, her Ladyship said: 29 The absence of the words the “last thing” or “step” in Rule 4.33 necessarily modifies the focus of the purposive and contextual assessment.
The issue is “advancing” or moving the action forward and what was done in the context of the real issues in dispute.
Accordingly, the court must take a macro view of what transpired in the three-year window.
That may require some dissection of what happened, and some examination of the dissected parts.
As Graesser J. noted in Le v 1055168 Alberta Ltd, the focus is on function, not whether an act fits into a defined category of activities.

30 Put another way, the court must view the whole picture of what transpired in the three-year period, framed by the real issues in dispute, and viewed through a lens trained on a qualitative assessment.
This necessarily involves assessing various factors including, but not limited to, the nature, value and quality, genuineness, timing, and in certain circumstances, the outcome of what occurred.
31 This approach does not affect the view that there is no difference between the words “materially advance” (in old Rule 244.1) and “significantly advance”.

However, it may affect the applicability of certain pre-November 1, 2013 authorities, particularly those that applied an analysis based on categories rather than functional impact. b. — The End Goal 32 Slatter J.A. commented in Windsor v Canadian Pacific Railway Ltd at para 15 that “the myth of trial should no longer govern civil procedure”.

The culture shift called for in Hryniak and echoed in Windsor supports the Plaintiff's contention that the end goal of “significant advancements” under Rule 4.33 is not necessarily trial, but rather resolution.
I agree.
33 The Rules employ the term “resolution” but do not define it.

In the context of litigation, the word often conjures images of “settlement” (“The reconciliation of conflicting views or parties in regard to a matter; the settlement of a dispute or conflict”: Oxford English Dictionary, online: <www.oed.com>).
Similarly, it can bring to mind a “disposition” (“A formal decision, determination, or expression of opinion by a deliberative assembly, committee, court …”: Oxford English Dictionary, online).
Both concepts exist on a litigation continuum ranging from abandonment of an action, to complete or partial settlement, to final disposition by ruling of the tribunal.

Final dispositions do not flow only from trials; they can take multiple forms ranging from striking of an unmeritorious action, dismissal of a dormant action, summary judgment or dismissal, summary trial, and a full trial.
While a full trial may be “a rarity” as Slatter J.A. observed in Windsor v Canadian Pacific Railway Ltd, for some it is nevertheless inevitable.
34 The Rules speak to dispute resolution with or without the court's assistance (Rule 15 (d)).

They place responsibility on the parties to manage their dispute, by engaging in good faith participation in alternate dispute resolution (Rule 4.16), and they mandate some form of dispute resolution (or Order waiving it) before a case can be set for trial (Rule 8.4(3)).
None of these notions existed until November 1, 2010 when the new Alberta Rules of Court came into force.

Their obvious purpose is to promote affordable, timely, and proportionate dispute resolution and to place squarely on litigants' shoulders the responsibility for working towards resolution of their lawsuit without the need for a trial.
35 The change in tenor of the new Rules supports the notion that litigation is no longer about reaching the ultimate goal of trial.
Rather, the goal—as stated in Hryniak and Windsor—is to resolve the case by proportionate means when it is just and fair to do so.
In St.
Jean Estate v.

Edmonton (City), 2014 ABQB 47, Topolniski, J. said, at paragraphs 18-19: 18 The current trend is to employ a functional approach to determine if an action moves the litigation forward in a meaningful way considering the nature, value, importance and quality of the action: Phillips v.
Sowan, 2007 ABCA 101, 40 CPC (6th) 378; Brar v.
Pawa, 2010 ABQB 779, 506 AR 325 (MC); Franchuk v.
Schick, 2013 ABQB 532, [2013] A.J.
No.
969 at para 12 (MC); Huynh v.
Rosman, 2013 ABQB 218 at paras 35-36, 42 CPC (7th) 301 (MC); Juke v.
John Doe, 2009 ABQB 557, 486 AR 254 (MC).
19 In other words, the focus is on substance and effect rather than form.
In Delorme v.

Canada (Attorney General), 2016 ABCA 168, 2016 CarswellAlta 1261, the majority of the Court said, at paragraph 27: 27 We agree with Topolniski J in Nash v Snow, 2014 ABQB 355 at para 32, 590 AR 198 that a “resolution” of disputes rather than a formal step leading to trial should be the premise upon which occurrences are judged as significant advancements.

We also agree with her comments in Nash at para 30: … the court must view the whole picture of what transpired in the three-year period, framed by the real issues in dispute, and viewed through a lens trained on a qualitative assessment.
This necessarily involves assessing various factors including, but not limited to, the nature, value and quality, genuineness, timing, and in certain circumstances, the outcome of what occurred.
In Huerto v.
Canniff, 2014 ABQB 534, 2014 CarswellAlta 1535; appeal dismissed 2015 ABCA 316, Madam Justice Shelley gave this summary of the law relating to R.

4.33: 20 Alberta courts have concluded that Rule 4.33 operates in a manner analogous to Alberta Rules of Court, Alta Reg 390/1968, Rule 244.1: Donnelly v Brick Warehouse Corp., 2013 ABQB 621 at paras 17-18; and Le v 1055168 Alberta Ltd., 2013 ABQB 431 at para 9.
The precursor Rule required a “material advance”, while Rule 4.33 tests delay on the absence of a “significant advance”.
This language is equivalent: Bahcheli v Yorkton Securities Inc., 2010 ABQB 824 at paras 26-27, 87 CCEL (3d) 80, affirmed 2012 ABCA 166, 524 AR 382.
Jurisprudence that considers and applies the pre-2010 Rule continues to be relevant, subject to the Rule 1.2 general interpretation provisions.
21 A “significant advance” is tested in a functional sense: does the step provide “meaningful” progress to the litigation?: Phillips v Sowan, 2007 ABCA 101, 40 CPC (6th) 378.

22 In Donnelly v Brick Warehouse Corp. at paras 19-20, Yamauchi J provides a helpful review of “things” that do or do not advance an action, which I expand below: a) steps that materially advance an action: • conducting examinations for discovery (or questioning): Lanset Capital Corp v Waterloo Geological Consulting Ltd, 2006 ABCA 77 at para 9, 380 AR 210; • complying with undertakings given pursuant to examinations for discovery (or questioning), subject to certain exceptions: Ravvin Holdings Ltd. v Ghitter, 2008 ABCA 208, 437 AR 66; and Gresiuk v Wawanesa Mutual Insurance Co

(2002), 316 AR 269 at 276–78 (Alta QB); • filing an affidavit of documents that sets out all of the relevant documents: Matthews v Great-West Life Assurance Co., 2002 ABQB 297, 313 AR 86; and Heikkila v Alberta (Workers' Compensation Board Appeals Commission), 2011 ABCA 87, 502 AR 243; • a pre-trial conference that identifies or addresses outstanding issues, or results in an order or court memorandum: Courtoreille v Edmonton (City), 2008 ABCA 90, 429 AR 58; • a process that streamlines or narrows the issues in dispute: 525812 Alberta Ltd v Purewal, 2004 ABQB 938 at para 16, 366 AR 1; • settlement negotiations that do not end the matter but narrow the issues between the parties: Montreal Trust Co. of Canada v Talcorp Ltd., [2013] A.J.
No.
770, at para 49; • a notice to admit that results in admissions: Nash v Snow, at para 51; and Bourne v Alberta, 2008 ABCA 165, 55 CPC

(6th) 1; and • gathering information that is material to resolve an issue, particularly where that information has been requested by or provided to the other party: Huynh v Rosman, 2013 ABQB 218 at paras 35–38, 40, 559 AR 319; see also Phillips v Sowan, 2007 ABCA 101 at para 6, 40 CPC

(6th) 378 for a specific example; b) steps that do not materially advance an action: • setting a date for examinations for discovery: Co-operators Life Insurance Co v Rollheiser, 1998 ABQB 874 at para 6, 231 AR 98;
